blocks.text: X-ray crystallography is a very strong analytical tool used to identify the three-dimensional positions of atoms in a crystalline solid. It is important in materials science, biochemistry and pharmaceutical chemistry because it lets scientists see the structures of materials. X-rays have a very small wavelength, so this radiation can be used to find the positions of electrons and atoms in a molecule or an ionic compound. Solid materials consist of layers or strands of atoms.
When X-rays from a source fall on a crystal, they are diffracted after hitting the atoms at specific angles (Figure 31.4).

blocks.alt: Two parallel incident X-rays (arrows) strike two neighbouring atoms in rows of red atoms one above the other, d apart, and leave as diffracted X-rays at the same angle theta to the rows. Pink perpendiculars from the upper atom cut off d sin theta on the lower ray before and after the lower atom; theta is marked at the upper atom and 2 theta at the lower atom. A pink bracket beside the diffracted rays is labelled '2d sin theta = total path length difference'.
blocks.caption: Figure 31.4: X-ray diffraction (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 31.4).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 31.4 labels the outgoing rays 'Different X-rays'; they are diffracted X-rays.

The diffracted rays make patterns on a screen called diffraction patterns. A diffraction pattern locates the atoms and electrons in a molecule; it can be turned into maps and gives the distances between atoms. Using mathematical models to analyse the pattern, scientists draw a detailed map of atomic positions and bond angles in the crystal, so the complete pattern of atoms and their electron density can be mapped to find the overall structure of the molecule or crystal. Figure 31.5 shows this for naphthalene.

blocks.alt: Left: an electron-density contour map of naphthalene: a thick outer contour with bumps where the hydrogen atoms are, two hexagonal holes in the middle of the rings, and nested rings of contours on the ten carbon atoms; leaders mark contours 500 (inner and outer), 1000 and 2000. Right: the structure of naphthalene, two fused six-membered rings with circles, ten C atoms and eight H atoms.
blocks.caption: Figure 31.5: The diffraction pattern of the naphthalene molecule (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 31.5).

blocks.text: The best-known use of X-ray diffraction (XRD) is the determination of the double helix structure of DNA. It is still used to analyse complex biomolecules such as enzymes and proteins. In drug development, designers use it to see how a drug molecule attaches to its target. It is also used to analyse minerals, synthetic crystals and nanomaterials, which helps improve material performance in electronics, optics and construction.
